extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; journalists studying historical newspaper practice
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and standards for judging or running mid-19th-century American newspapers (editorial, ethical, business, and news-practice dimensions) as described in a history-of-the-press chapter. Useful for historians, journalism students, or anyone assessing period newspapers' quality and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation and reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured by subscription and distribution numbers (daily and weekly circulation figures are cited as indicators of success and influence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Weekly Tribune reached 200,000 by 1860; Tribune daily had about 45,000 subscribers pre-Civil War; Log Cabin campaign paper sold 85,000. The text treats large and growing circulation—especially wide weekly distribution—as a core measure of a paper's national influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing and business model (cheap-for-cash penny papers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper's price point and financing model (penny/cheap-for-cash, later increases to two cents) determine affordability, scale, and sustainability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: Many papers began at one cent then raised price to two cents—this could temporarily reduce circulation but allow more pages and financial viability. Capital needs and mechanical plant costs (e.g., Times capitalized at $100,000) influence editorial choices and longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution methods (London plan, club rates, premiums)
rubrics_metrics.description: How a paper distributes and markets itself—selling to carriers (London plan), club subscription rates, and use of premiums—affects penetration into towns and rural areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance from text: clubs of twenty could obtain discounted rates (e.g., $1), premiums and club systems made weeklies popular in small cities and towns and helped broaden readership beyond urban centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: News-gathering enterprise and technical innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Active investment in faster and better news collection and mechanical techniques (special expresses, telegraph use, typesetting aboard steamers, foreign correspondents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tribune financed special expresses, used typesetting aboard Hudson River steamers, adopted telegraph news to strengthen departments, and the Times sent Raymond abroad to cover war—such enterprise expedited news and distinguished papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local news focus and strong telegraph department
rubrics_metrics.description: Devotion to local news and local interests, combined with telegraph reporting, can give a paper distinction and steady growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samuel Bowles III made the Springfield Republican notable by stressing local news and telegraph items; strong local/telegraph departments are credited as key departments for identity and readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, straightforward news-writing (condensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear, condensed prose and avoidance of wordiness are presented as a stylistic standard for effective news journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bowles is praised for making his paper famous for ‘straightforward, concise news-writing’; the text contrasts this with the ‘wordiness of the current literary style’ as an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary miscellany and regular review departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of literary material (essays, serial fiction, poetry) and dedicated departments (e.g., regular book reviews) as markers of editorial breadth and prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribune established a regular department for book reviews and serialized literature; such features increased prestige and attracted broader, especially weekly, readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff quality and notable contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: The caliber of the editorial and writing staff (distinguished contributors, skilled managing editors) is a criterion of a paper's overall quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: George Ripley, Margaret Fuller, Bayard Taylor, Charles A. Dana contributed to the Tribune; the chapter calls the Tribune's staff 'the most brilliant staff any American newspaper had yet assembled.' Strong staff lifts both news and literary quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial influence and leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity of the editorial page to lead, form, and shape public opinion—‘influence’ versus organizational ‘leadership’—is an evaluative dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text distinguishes leadership (crystallizing and organizing opinion) from influence (forming and controlling attitudes). Greeley's Tribune is described as having extraordinary influence in shaping public opinion and national causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy and editorial causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of editorials to champion social, political, and economic causes (antislavery, Maine law, opposition to capital punishment, homestead law, internal improvements, labor issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greeley's persistent campaigns (e.g., antislavery, westward expansion, homestead law) are cited as central to the Tribune’s role. The rubric implies that sustained, well-argued advocacy is a measure of editorial impact, though it should be situated within broader movements and other actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for novel ideas and intellectual openness
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper's willingness to 'accord a generous welcome to every novel suggestion' and to publish a range of reformist or experimental ideas is a positive editorial trait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greeley's stated aim to welcome novel suggestions and unselfish efforts is highlighted. The text frames openness as a virtue even if many ideas prove erroneous—rejection of potentially improving ideas is discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between moral stance and commercial/advertising pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which a paper maintains stated moral/ethical positions in the face of business pressures (advertising revenue, ownership influence) is an evaluative dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Tribune’s aversion to 'immoral and degrading Police Reports, Advertisements' but later acceptance of certain ads and yielding to business-office pressure. The text treats the tension as common and important to assess when judging a paper's ethical consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical approach to crime and sensational reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies on publishing lurid or detailed crime reports and sensational material reflect ethical editorial standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribune initially condemned publishing 'loathsome details' of murder trials, yet later used elaborate reporting of the Colt murder case to build circulation. Anti-pattern: exploiting sensational crime detail to boost sales; best practice: restraint and principled reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial style: vigor, terseness, clarity, and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stylistic qualities of editorials and prose—vigor, terseness, clearness, and simplicity—are valued as indicators of effective editorial voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary praise compared Greeley’s style to Cobbett for vigor and terseness. The text implies that such an English style contributes to influence and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy and emphasis on foreign news coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope and quality of foreign news reporting and the willingness to send correspondents abroad are measures of a paper’s comprehensiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Times’ emphasis on foreign affairs and Raymond’s dispatch to Italy (war correspondent) are cited as establishing a pattern for preeminence; broad foreign coverage strengthens a paper’s national reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of campaign papers and partisan publishing tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Employment of campaign papers, low-priced partisan sheets, and organized propaganda as tools for political influence and electioneering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaign papers (e.g., Jeffersonian, Log Cabin) were published to support candidates (Seward, Harrison) and could be highly effective—Log Cabin sold 85,000 for six months. The rubric notes their role in political mobilization but also their transient/campaign-limited nature.
